title: Bhopal Scientists Build India's First Indigenous H5N1 Vaccine for Chickens
excerpt: ICAR-NIHSAD's inactivated vaccine targets clade 2.3.2.1a, the strain behind most Indian bird flu outbreaks, and is expected to cost around Rs 1-2 a dose once it is manufactured.
body:
• ICAR-NIHSAD in Bhopal has developed India's first indigenous inactivated H5N1 vaccine for chickens, targeting clade 2.3.2.1a, the strain behind most bird flu outbreaks in Indian poultry.
  • Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan dedicated the vaccine to the nation on November 20, 2026, and indicated an expected cost of around Rs 1-2 per dose.
  • In experimental trials, a primary dose followed by a booster after 21 days protected chickens, and the virus did not spread to unvaccinated birds kept in contact with vaccinated ones.
  • There is no on-farm availability date yet: wider use depends on technology transfer, manufacturing and regulatory arrangements.

India now has a bird flu vaccine of its own. Scientists at the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD) in Bhopal have developed the country's first indigenous inactivated vaccine against the H5N1 virus for chickens, and Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan dedicated it to the nation on November 20, 2026.

"The government has also announced a proposed BSL-4 laboratory at ICAR-NIHSAD in Bhopal, estimated to cost Rs 300 crore, to expand India's capacity for research on high-risk animal pathogens."

What the vaccine is

The vaccine targets H5N1 clade 2.3.2.1a. Avian influenza viruses fall into different genetic groups, and studies cited by the Press Information Bureau show this clade has been responsible for most bird flu outbreaks in Indian chickens. No specific commercial vaccine against this clade was available before, the PIB said. Because the formulation is inactivated, it uses killed virus to train the bird's immune system rather than live infectious virus. The schedule is a primary dose followed by a booster after 21 days.

The research began in September 2025 and the vaccine was developed in August 2026 under stringent biosafety conditions at NIHSAD, ICAR's institute for high-risk animal diseases, according to Hindusthan Samachar. In a contact-transmission experiment, vaccinated chickens were kept alongside unvaccinated birds and researchers reported the virus did not spread to the unvaccinated birds. The institute's results come from controlled experimental conditions; performance on commercial farms, where flock size, housing and exposure levels vary, will need field evidence.

Why it matters

Highly pathogenic avian influenza can cause nearly 100 per cent mortality among infected birds, and control has meant large-scale culling and trade restrictions. Since H5N1 was first detected in India in 2006, more than 500 combined outbreaks of H5N1 and H5N8 have been reported in the country, according to the Agriculture Ministry. The 2006 outbreak caused estimated direct and indirect losses of Rs 2,200-3,000 crore, and the ministry estimates more than 20 per cent of the country's poultry population could be at risk if the disease spreads without control. H5N1 is also a public health concern: the World Health Organization counts 1,003 human cases, including 479 deaths, across 25 countries since 2003. This vaccine is for chickens, not humans — its public-health value lies in reducing how much virus circulates in poultry.

What happens next

Technology transfer arrangements were taken up during the November 20 programme, and Chouhan indicated an expected cost of around Rs 1-2 per dose, with affordability for poultry farmers an important consideration. That figure is an indicative estimate: the final price and availability will depend on manufacturing and distribution arrangements, and no rollout date has been announced. The government has also announced a proposed BSL-4 laboratory at ICAR-NIHSAD in Bhopal, estimated to cost Rs 300 crore, to expand India's capacity for research on high-risk animal pathogens.
nri_angle: A home-grown, low-cost bird flu vaccine strengthens disease control for India's poultry sector, on which egg and chicken prices and farmer livelihoods depend.
